articles.title: Sound waves could help stop schizophrenic delusions: NYU study
articles.description: Scientists at NYU have conducted a successful experiment on 10 schizophrenic patients using sound waves directed into a tiny region deep inside the brain called the globus pallidus interna. The experiment resulted in a proven reduction of symptoms and causes new help for future treatments.

articles.title: Scientists discover a hidden flaw that challenges 40 years of superconductor science
articles.description: A superconducting material studied for 40 years has turned out to be far more complex than scientists believed. Advanced 3D imaging revealed a hidden patchwork of crystal structures, with unusually wide boundaries that may weaken superconductivity. The discovery challenges decades of scientific assumptions and could explain why some superconductors outperform others.

articles.title: ‘Start that conversation’: Saskatchewan Science Centre aiming to educate public on nuclear power
articles.description: As part of Nuclear Science Week, the Saskatchewan Science Centre set up various booths on Saturday to help educate the public on the topic.

articles.title: From Russian cages to Irish sanctuary: The five-year rescue journey of Bu and Tyapa
articles.description: For Bu and Tyapa, the five-year journey from Russia to the Irish countryside was anything but straightforward.

articles.title: Bell pepper colors reveal differences in sweetness, nutrients and ripeness
articles.description: Raw, grilled, roasted, stuffed—there are many ways to enjoy bell peppers, also called capsicums, sweet peppers or paprika. Bell peppers originated in Central and South America and belong to the nightshade family along with tomatoes and eggplants.

articles.title: Tests reveal why titanium additions do not fully prevent pitting corrosion in stainless steel
articles.description: Stainless steel is widely used for its corrosion resistance, but it is not invincible. In environments containing chloride ions, such as seawater, pitting corrosion can occur. These pits often start at tiny particles called inclusions embedded in the steel.

articles.title: Hear Amelia Earhart's VOICE like never before: Scientists use AI to enhance a recording logged two years before the pilot's disappearance
articles.description: Scientists have used AI to enhance a historical recording of Amelia Earhart, making her voice sound clearer than ever before.

articles.title: Single X-ray pulse reveals plasma nanostructures across scales with one camera
articles.description: Understanding instabilities and turbulence in plasmas is one of the key challenges across a wide range of plasma research fields, including nuclear fusion, astrophysics and laser-plasma physics. In plasmas, slight disturbances can grow due to instabilities, and energy is transferred between structures of various sizes due to turbulence. These phenomena give rise to structures ranging from very small to large, which significantly influence the overall motion and energy flow of the plasma.

articles.title: 'One-positron cyclotron' could test a key prediction of the Standard Model
articles.description: The positron is the antimatter counterpart of the electron, identical in mass but carrying an equal and opposite electric charge. Like the electron, it also behaves like a tiny bar magnet, and according to a key prediction of the Standard Model of particle physics, its magnetic moment should be exactly equal and opposite to the electron's.

articles.description: Moderna and Merck's 'presidential' presentation, and other news from Day 2 of the European Society for Medical Oncology meeting in Madrid.

articles.title: Newly identified protein pathway helps HIV stay hidden despite treatment
articles.description: Current HIV medicines are effective at suppressing the virus in the blood. However, HIV can remain "asleep" or dormant inside certain immune cells and in the brain. These hidden pockets of virus, called HIV reservoirs, are the main reason HIV cannot be cured with today's treatments.

articles.title: Can power consumption reveal whether a data center is secretly training AI?
articles.description: Research | The core idea is simple and surprisingly clever: when a data center trains a large AI model, the training process leaves a characteristic pattern in its power consumption. This pattern could be measured externally to detect undisclosed training runs. This is important for the governance of large AI data centers, the enforcement of potential restrictions, and related oversight efforts.

articles.description: What seabirds eat might seem like a good starting point for identifying species that tend to accumulate plastic in their digestive systems. articles.description: A groundbreaking study challenges 70 years of assumptions about how human language works. By analyzing billions of word uses, scientists discovered that meaning is organized around power, danger, and order rather than emotion alone. Even more surprisingly, human language shows a powerful hidden preference for safety, suggesting that our words may reflect ancient survival instincts.

articles.title: Austen is for everyone: Sense and Sensibility (2026)
articles.description: Like a warm beverage on a crisp autumn evening, Georgia Oakley's Sense and Sensibility (2026) is the perfect girls-night-in film as the temperature drops here in Baltimore. While some Austen purists may be clutching their pearls, as a casual Austen fan I had a wonderful time with the newest adaptation of the classic novel. This movie captures her characteristic wit and charm and brings it to the modern era of cinema. The 1811 novel centers around the Dashwood family, particularly the romantic entanglements of the eldest daughters Elinor (Daisy Edgar-Jones) and Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles), as they deal with their newfound financial difficulties after the death of their father. Elinor, the eldest represents sense with her endless pragmatism and restraint, and Marianne represents sensibility with her intense passion and romantic idealism. While the story follows each of their romances, an argument can be made that the real love story is that of Elinor and Marianne - something Oakley highlights. Throughout the novel, Marianne grows to have a bit more sense and Elinor becomes a bit more sensible. The film is rooted in its characters, and both actresses make for deeply personable leads. I knew going in that Edgar-Jones (of Normal People fame) would capture the audience's attention, but Creed-Miles fully holds her own as the wild, tempestuous Marianne. George MacKay is also the perfect choice for Edward, Elinor's love interest. With a piercing gaze and incredibly English features (in The-Year-of-Zendaya/Robert Pattinson/Anne Hathaway, I'm so grateful I've never seen his face before), he delivers the yearning now mandatory for a romance. Fiona Shaw also steals the show as the endlessly prattling Mrs. Jennings. She turns what I had expected to be a strictly comedic-relief role into a memorably endearing one. Everyone is familiar with the 2005 Pride and Prejudice (if you haven't seen the film, you've definitely seen a clip of the Darcy hand-flex); among Austen fans, the 1995 Sense and Sensibility film starring Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet is truly beloved (not to mention its 7 Academy Award nominations and win for Best Adapted Screenplay), so Oakley had big shoes to fill. She took visual inspiration from the 2005 classic, with rich sepia tones and vast natural landscapes, but made it her own with some interesting parallel compositions. In the era of remakes, the film is an adaptation done right, with changes to the plot only in service of the greater story (Wuthering Heights, I'm looking at you). The reason these stories remain so popular is that they tackle universal themes of sisterhood, romantic misunderstanding and integrity, and they do not need significant adjusting in order to be relatable to modern audiences. Elinor has a grand romantic moment running after Edward to clarify a misunderstanding, which never happened in the book, but is a neat way to conclude her arc as a person learning to express her feelings. Edward was also made much more likeable in this iteration than the 1995 version (what can I say, Hugh Grant doesn't do it for me), which helps us root for our main leads. While the script is not the most subtle in its wit, it is a homage to Austen's famously biting and clever dialogue which left me laughing all the way through. Unfortunately, the duel scene between Brandon and Willoughby (Marianne's love interests) near the end felt off both in tone and in score, likely because this happened off-page in the book. Also, try as I might to ignore it, I did find Marianne's unkempt hair distractedly disheveled at times. As on-brand for her character as it was, it seemed odd because the rest of the film seems to capture the 18th century so well (aside from the dances, for which I'll defer to an expert). There has been some discourse about historical accuracy in these period pieces (see: Bridgerton). While this one is definitely not perfect, as she discusses in this interview with IndieWire, costume designer Grace Snell highlights how the two sisters learn from one another in the way they dress over the course of the story: Elinor with more ribbons and Marianne with more structure. Oakley's choices were in service to her characters rather than the time period, and as a casual viewer, I'd say it worked. Sense and Sensibility wasn't a life-changing film, nor do I see it winning an Academy Award like its predecessor, but it was a cozy one - warm and easy and comforting in all the right ways - and definitely worth watching whenever it comes to streaming, regardless of your familiarity with the source material.

articles.title: Ways to Stay Healthy This Flu Season
articles.description: Happy autumn, Blue Jays! While the leaves falling down and the chillier weather are exciting, this is also a time where many students get sick. Whether it be a fever, headache, or sore throat, catching an illness is not a fun time. To try and avoid this, here are a few tips from me on how to not get sick and how to recover quickly if you do. To prevent sickness: 1) Drink water Sounds cliche, I know. But the #1 thing you can do, in my opinion, to stay healthy is consume lots of fluids, preferably room temperature or heated. Drinking water has SO many benefits, and it's free. a. Kidney health Trust me, you want your kidneys to be healthy no matter what. Kidney stones are about the most painful things you can experience. b. Metabolism Fills up your stomach and helps regulate your metabolism and temperature. Water prevents overeating and maintains balance of body fluids. c. Skin health Drinking water keeps your skin looking glowy and soft. d. Digestion Feeling bloated? Drink hot water! This acts as a lubricant for your organs and heats you up from the inside. e. Keeps you warm Drinking warm or hot water combats the cold weather. This in itself keeps you from getting sick. 2) Layer up Remember when you were a kid and your mom always told you to bring an extra jacket? This might've been annoying at the time, but she was right. It's always a good idea to layer up, and it's much better to err on the side of too hot instead of too cold. You can always remove layers but you can't add them if you didn't bring them! Some ways to do this are: - Layering leggings underneath baggy jeans - Layering long sleeves or turtlenecks underneath sweaters, crewnecks, or hoodies - Always bringing an extra jacket 3) Get enough sleep I'm lucky enough to be in Introduction to Psychology (shoutout Chaz Firestone the goat), and this past week we learned about the vast importance of sleep. In fact, sleep is more effective for concentration than caffeine and the abuse of stimulants such as Adderall. Getting enough sleep helps your immune system because it gives it enough energy to fight a potential illness. Feeling happier and more well rested after sleep can also improve overall health. If you do get sick, here are some ways to ensure a speedy recovery: 1) Drink ginger tea!! This was a tip made by my mom, who always made this whenever my siblings and I got sick. She would boil cut up ginger with water, and we would drink the spicy concoction, bundle up and fall asleep sweating. Although this sounds odd, it has always worked. I don't know how feasible this is in a dorm room, although it's possible that Charles Street Market sells ginger. 2) Gargle salt water This tip works best if you have a sore throat. Have you ever woken up and swallowed and it hurt? Terrible experience. Mix about 1 teaspoon of salt into warm water and gargle for 30-60 seconds for temporary relief. 3) Bundle up Always dress more heavily than you should. Sweating helps the illness go away, and staying warm is a top priority. Do not go outside with wet hair, and try to cover your body with hats (like a beanie) and scarves or turtlenecks. Wear gloves and long socks as well. Please take care of yourselves!! Remember, your health is always a top priority over anything else. If you feel something is wrong, get it checked out before it is too late. There are plenty of free resources provided to you on campus that are waiting to be utilized. I hope these tips are helpful, and I wish you guys the best of luck this flu season.

articles.title: Child-led citizen science helps Ecuadorian community tackle beach pollution and shape environmental decisions
articles.description: Pollution from human-generated waste in marine ecosystems has reached critical levels, with cigarette butts (CBs) among the most persistent and harmful pollutants. Globally, an estimated 4.5 trillion cigarette butts are discarded annually, making them the most common type of litter on beaches over the past three decades.

articles.title: White Dwarfs Are Actually…Yellow, Green, Pink, and Purple?
articles.description: The universe hosts a myriad of star types, including supergiants, giants, main sequence, red dwarfs, brown dwarfs, white dwarfs, and neutron stars. What makes these stars stand out are just their sizes, but their colors, as each one hosts a distinct color based on their surface temperature, specifically orange, red, blue, and white based on cooler to hotter temperatures. While the correlation between star colors and surface temperatures has long been known throughout astronomy, what if star colors could change based on specific criteria, including their atmosphere?

articles.title: Habitat explains Finnish animal distributions better than climate, study finds
articles.description: Researchers at the University of Helsinki wanted to understand which is the dominant factor for species occurrence and abundance: the climate or habitat-related variables, such as their natural state and the share of land shaped by human activity. Solutions to mitigate biodiversity loss depend on the answer to this question.

articles.title: Power cuts and sleep: Students link load shedding to anxiety, disrupted rest and lower grades
articles.description: South Africa endured its worst year of load shedding (scheduled power cuts by the country's utility, Eskom) in 2023. The power went off on 335 of the year's 365 days, often several times a day. Since then, the country has gone more than a year and a half without these planned power cuts.

articles.title: NASA Is Still Aiming for the Next Moon Landing in 2028
articles.description: Administrator Jared Isaacman said that the space agency was exploring ways to keep Artemis III on target without compromising safety.

articles.title: Glowing plants reveal immune responses around infection sites via two colors
articles.description: Researchers at the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (LMS) have developed a new way to make glowing biological reporters more accurate, allowing scientists to track gene activity in living plants over days, weeks and potentially even months and years. The approach could help researchers study how plants respond to disease, pests and environmental stress, while opening the door to similar applications in animal and human disease models.

articles.title: 27 Exoplanet Targets for the World's First Private Space Telescope
articles.description: Get ready for the age of private space telescopes. The Lazuli Space Telescope will launch in a few years and part of its mission is to observe exoplanets. New research presents a list of 27 exoplanet targets, some of which are very well-known and will certainly benefit from deeper observations.

articles.title: Study maps the human side of flood risk
articles.description: When heavy rain hits a city, knowing where water will accumulate is only part of the picture. Who lives in the affected buildings? How might flooding disrupt their lives? And where could additional support make the greatest difference?

articles.title: AI-Powered Wearable Device Could One Day Transmit Smells Over the Internet
articles.description: Learn how a wearable device can recreate smells transmitted over the internet, potentially bringing a new sensory dimension to virtual experiences.

articles.title: Mount Erebus Is One of Earth's Most Unusual Volcanoes, With a Rare Lava Lake and Chimney-Like Towers
articles.description: Learn more about Mount Erebus, why it's so unique, and what modern technology has told us about it.

articles.title: Plain silicon grating reveals a hidden 'twist' in light from electron beams
articles.description: In 1953, two physicists showed that an electron beam skimming past a grating emits light whose color depends only on the electron's speed and the grating's spacing. Known as Smith-Purcell radiation, this phenomenon has become a useful tool for building compact, tunable light sources and tracking particle beams without touching them.
